challenges: Maintaining parameter efficiency while achieving high classification accuracy was a primary challenge. Optimizing the LoRA rank (r=6) and alpha (α=24) parameters to stay within a 1 million trainable parameter budget required iterative experimentation. Misclassification between Business and Sci/Tech categories due to semantic overlap was another challenge addressed through detailed evaluation of class-wise metrics and confusion matrices.
detailed_description: This project implemented a text classification model using the RoBERTa-base architecture, fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient training. Conducted as part of the Deep Learning course at NYU in Spring 2025, the model was trained on the AG News dataset, which contains approximately 120,000 articles across four categories: World, Sports, Business, and Sci/Tech. The LoRA configuration focused on adapting the query, key, and value matrices within attention layers while freezing the rest of the model. We utilized a warmup-based linear learning rate scheduler, early stopping mechanism, and PyTorch-based DataLoader pipelines. The final model achieved a test accuracy of 94.59% with only 925,444 trainable parameters, amounting to 0.737% of the full model size. Evaluation involved visualizing training metrics, confusion matrices, and F1 scores per class, followed by Kaggle test submission.

RoBERTa-base architecture with frozen base weights
Targeted adaptation of query, key, value matrices
Early stopping based on validation loss
Linear LR scheduling with 10% warmup steps
Visualization of training/validation metrics and confusion matrix
Class-wise F1 score analysis and normalized confusion matrix
learnings: Learned to implement LoRA with the PEFT library for targeted attention adaptation. Gained insights into configuring AdamW optimizer, learning rate warmup, and linear decay. Developed understanding of data preprocessing for text classification tasks, including tokenization, attention masking, and max-length truncation. Practiced model evaluation using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Understood how to reduce memory footprint through selective fine-tuning of transformer layers. Also gained hands-on experience with Hugging Face datasets and integrating the Transformers library in PyTorch.
short_description: Efficient text classification using RoBERTa fine-tuned with LoRA on the AG News dataset, achieving high accuracy with minimal trainable parameters.
title: RoBERTa-LoRA News Classification

detailed_description: This project, developed as part of the Machine Learning course at NYU Tandon, focuses on predicting investment behavior on Shark Tank US using historical data of over 1,360 startup pitches from 16 seasons. The goal was to analyze investor preferences and develop machine learning models capable of predicting both the likelihood and the amount of investment by individual sharks. The project involved preprocessing a complex dataset with missing values, handling class imbalance using SMOTE, and applying feature engineering techniques such as OpenAI embedding models for textual fields. Multiple classification (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) and regression (Random Forest Regressor, XGBoost Regressor) models were developed, tuned, and evaluated using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, RMSE, and R². XGBoost emerged as the best-performing model. Visualizations, industry trend analysis, and shark-specific patterns further enriched the insights provided by the models.

detailed_description: As part of a deep learning project at New York University, we designed and implemented a custom ResNet-based image classifier targeting the CIFAR-10 dataset. The primary aim was to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy within a parameter constraint of 5 million. Our architecture combined Pre-Activation ResNet blocks with Mish activation, CBAM attention modules, and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) blocks. We integrated a transformer block for capturing global dependencies and employed strong regularization methods like label smoothing and CutMix. Training utilized the AdamW optimizer and a OneCycleLR scheduler across 200+ epochs. With advanced augmentations and test-time augmentation (TTA), our model achieved a 95.60% validation accuracy. This project solidified practical skills in deep model engineering, data augmentation, and scalable PyTorch training pipelines.

challenges: Key challenges included maintaining valid pixel ranges during iterative attacks and tuning hyperparameters like epsilon, alpha, and momentum for effective performance. The Patch attack introduced high computational overhead due to multiple optimization restarts. Ensuring consistent evaluation required careful handling of model determinism. Visualizing subtle perturbations clearly and assessing transferability across architectures like ResNet and DenseNet also added complexity, particularly when aligning each attack's constraints with model behavior.
detailed_description: This research-driven project evaluated the adversarial vulnerability of deep neural network classifiers, specifically ResNet-34 and DenseNet-121, using four types of attacks: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), Momentum Iterative FGSM (MI-FGSM), and Patch attacks. Experiments were conducted on a subset of the ImageNet-1K dataset with 500 images spanning 100 classes. Each attack was designed and implemented in PyTorch using torchvision pre-trained models. Evaluation included both white-box and black-box scenarios to test transferability of attacks. The project revealed significant degradation in model accuracy, with PGD reducing ResNet-34 Top-1 accuracy from 77.40% to 0.00%. Patch attacks demonstrated strong transferability despite localized perturbations. The project also included detailed visualizations and comparison plots to showcase the impact and effectiveness of adversarial techniques.

Evaluated adversarial robustness on ResNet-34 and DenseNet-121

Analyzed attack transferability between architectures

Hyperparameter tuning for effective attack strength
Comprehensive comparative results across attack types
learnings: We gained practical experience implementing adversarial attacks using PyTorch and analyzing model vulnerabilities in deep learning. The project deepened our understanding of hyperparameter tuning, image preprocessing, and top-k evaluation metrics. We also developed skills in visualizing adversarial effects and understanding how attacks transfer between different architectures, reinforcing the need for robust model design.
short_description: Explored adversarial robustness of ResNet-34 and DenseNet-121 using FGSM, PGD, MI-FGSM, and Patch attacks on ImageNet subset.
title: Adversarial Attacks on ResNet and DenseNet

detailed_description: This project was developed in a 24-hour state-level technical hackathon by a team of four students. The core idea was to reduce road accidents by addressing drowsiness while driving. The system uses a basic webcam or USB camera to monitor the driver's eye activity. By using simple computer vision techniques, it identifies if the driver’s eyes remain closed beyond a typical blink duration. If this happens more than three times within a short span, the device sends an SMS alert to a pre-registered emergency contact, warning them of the driver’s condition. The project was designed using pre-trained facial landmark detection models available in OpenCV along with Python scripting. The alert mechanism used basic integration with an SMS API like Twilio. The focus was on demonstrating a working proof-of-concept within the limited time of a hackathon, which helped us deliver a functional prototype with real-time response.
